claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are governed by interactions among lattice distortion, grain-boundary segregation, and dislocation dynamics.
Integrating in-situ TEM with molecular-dynamics simulations can reveal how these factors govern hardness and strength.
The proposed hypothesis applies to as-cast or annealed high-entropy alloys.
Uniaxial tensile testing or nanoindentation at ambient temperature and pressure is the proposed intervention.
Deformation rates will be controlled during testing.
Lattice distortion, grain-boundary segregation, and dislocation dynamics influence dislocation mobility.
Lattice distortion, grain-boundary segregation, and dislocation dynamics influence grain-boundary strength.
Changes in dislocation mobility and grain-boundary strength control the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys.
Increasing lattice distortion will increase hardness and strength.
Increasing grain-boundary segregation will increase hardness and strength.
Increasing dislocation mobility will decrease hardness and strength.
A reference high-entropy alloy with known composition and microstructure will serve as the baseline.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys containing 5–13 principal elements.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for grain sizes between 100 and 1000 nm.
The hypothesis is limited to ambient temperature and pressure.
A failure of the measured mediators to correlate with the predicted changes in hardness and strength would falsify the hypothesis.
